The application itself was straightforward, but the supporting materials took longer than expected. I included:

1. A cover letter addressed to the GSS Accreditation Committee

**Items still pending for the GSS review:**
- Final version of the submission checklist (due 22 March)
- Updated community engagement section (Evelyn said she could help with this)
- Any additional documentation the committee requests after their initial review

---

**Marriage Record — Lim Family (1892):**

I found the marriage record at the National Archives yesterday afternoon. It was in the Straits Settlements records, which makes sense given the time period. The record is dated 12 June 1892, and it lists:

- Groom: Lim Ah Kow (age 26, merchant)
- Bride: Tan Swee Neo (age 19, no occupation listed)
- Witnesses: Lim Cheng Hoe and Tan Kim Seng
- Location: St. Andrew's Cathedral, Singapore

This is significant because it connects the Lim and Tan families directly. I've been trying to establish this connection for months.

**Next steps for this line:**
- Cross-reference with the church records at St. Andrew's (the National Archives copy is a transcription, so I need to check the original)
- Look for the couple's marriage certificate in the Registrar-General's records
- Search for birth records of their children (likely 1893–1910)

---

**Tan Family Branch — Progress Update:**

Evelyn sent me an email this morning with a lead on the Tan family. She found a reference to "Tan Swee Neo" in a 1905 directory of Singapore merchants. The directory lists her as the widow of Lim Ah Kow, which confirms that Lim Ah Kow died sometime between 1892 and 1905.

On 15 March, Marcus Lim submitted_application_to Genealogical Society of Singapore. Record status: current.

**Key details from the directory:**
- Name: Tan Swee Neo (widow of Lim Ah Kow)
- Address: 14 Telok Ayer Street
- Occupation: Merchant (continuing her husband's business)
- Notes: Listed as "proprietor of Lim Ah Kow & Co."

This is useful, but I need to find the exact date of Lim Ah Kow's death. I'll check the burial records at Bukit Brown Cemetery and the Straits Settlements death records.

**Possible leads:**
- Bukit Brown Cemetery records (available at the National Archives)
- Straits Settlements death records (1880–1910)
- Probate records for Lim Ah Kow (likely in the Supreme Court records)

---

**DNA Test Results — Interpretation:**

I received the DNA test results from the lab earlier this week. The results are for the sample I submitted in February (sample ID: LFHP-DNA-2024-02).

**Summary of results:**
- Y-DNA haplogroup: O-M122 (common in southern China)
- mtDNA haplogroup: M7 (also common in southern China)
- Autosomal DNA: 92% East Asian, 5% Southeast Asian, 3% unassigned

**Interpretation notes:**
- The Y-DNA haplogroup is consistent with the Lim family's documented origins in Fujian Province, China
- The mtDNA haplogroup suggests the maternal line also originated in southern China
- The 5% Southeast Asian component could indicate some degree of local admixture — this is worth investigating further

**Caveats:**
- These results are statistical estimates, not definitive proof of ancestry
- The unassigned 3% may resolve with future updates to the reference database
- I should compare these results with the samples from other family members (Evelyn's father and my cousin) when they arrive

The NAS website indicated a 10-working-day turnaround for this series, which would have been around 24 May. I have not yet received an email confirmation that the records are ready. I will call the NAS reference desk on Monday, 3 June, at 10:00 SGT to check on the status.

She also mentioned that the lab is in the process of updating their reference database, which may refine the unassigned 3% in the autosomal results. She expects the update to be completed by the end of June.

I will note in the DNA log that the results should be re-checked after the database update, and I will compare with Marcus's sample once it arrives.

- **Marcus's sample (tracking number SG-7842-1190):** Confirmed delivered to the California lab on 5 June (Pacific Time). The lab sent an acknowledgment on 6 June (SGT). I have filed the acknowledgment in the DNA correspondence folder.

**Newspaper Search — Death Date of Lim Ah Kow**

I began the digitized newspaper search on Monday, 3 June, as planned. I have been using the National Library's NewspaperSG portal from home. So far I have searched the *Straits Times* and *Malaya Tribune* for the period 1928–1932, using the search terms "Lim Ah Kow" and "Lim A Kow" (the latter spelling appears in some early records).

The search is slow because the OCR quality is poor for the 1920s issues, and there are many false positives (the name is common). I have narrowed the search to obituary notices and death announcements. I have found two possible matches, both in the *Malaya Tribune*:

- 14 March 1930: A death notice for a "Lim Ah Kow" of Kampong Java Road, aged 61. This could be our Lim Ah Kow, but the age does not match the 1911 birth certificate (which would make him 19 in 1930). I have noted this as a low-priority lead.
- 22 November 1931: A death notice for a "Lim Ah Kow" of River Valley Road. The age is not stated. I have requested a clearer scan of this page from the National Library; the request reference is NL/REF/2024/0831.
I followed up with Dr. Natalie Wong at the California lab in early September, as I had planned. The reference database update she expected in June was delayed, but it finally went live on 2 September. She re-ran the Y-DNA haplogroup analysis for Marcus's sample. The result remains O-M122, which is consistent with the Fujian origin. She also noted that the subclade prediction has improved slightly — the new database suggests a more specific branch (O-M122\* with a possible link to the Minnan cluster), but she cautioned that the resolution is still not sufficient for a confident subclade assignment. She recommended we consider a deeper SNP test in the new year if we want to narrow the geographic origin further. I have added this to the list of pending tasks for Q1 2025.

Evelyn's autosomal results have also been updated. The unassigned 3% that we had been tracking has now been resolved: 2% is assigned to the "Southern China" reference population, and 1% remains unassigned. Dr. Wong explained that this residual unassigned portion is common for individuals with significant admixture from historically underrepresented populations. No further action is needed on this.

**Newspaper Search — Death Date of Lim Ah Kow**

The search for Lim Ah Kow's death date has been a slow but steady process. Since my last entry, I have continued working through the digitised newspapers on NewspaperSG, focusing on the *Straits Times* and *Malaya Tribune* for the period 1932–1935. The two leads I noted in June have both been resolved:

- The 14 March 1930 death notice for a "Lim Ah Kow" of Kampong Java Road, aged 61, is not our man. The age does not match, and the address, while in the same area, is not one we have linked to the family. I have marked this lead as closed.
- The 22 November 1931 death notice for a "Lim Ah Kow" of River Valley Road remains a strong lead. The clearer scan I requested from the National Library (reference NL/REF/2024/0831) arrived on 12 September. The notice reads: "Lim Ah Kow, of 14 River Valley Road, passed away peacefully at his residence on 21 November 1931, aged 44. Funeral to leave on 23 November at 3 p.m." The age of 44 would be consistent with a birth year of 1887, which does not match our Lim Ah Kow (born 1911). However, I have not ruled it out entirely, because the death notice may have been placed by a relative with the same name. I have requested the death certificate from the Registry of Births and Deaths; the reference is RBD/2024/1042. I expect a response within two weeks.

I have also searched for obituaries in the *Singapore Free Press* and the *Pinang Gazette* for the period 1928–1935, but the OCR quality is poor and the search has not yielded any new leads. I will pause the newspaper search until the death certificate request comes back.

**Correspondence with the Genealogical Society of Singapore (GSS)**

In August, I wrote to the GSS to ask about their records of Chinese clan associations in Singapore, particularly the Lim Kongsi (clan association) records for the early 20th century. The GSS replied on 18 September with a letter (reference GSS/REF/2024/123) explaining that the clan association records are not held by the GSS but are kept by the individual associations. They provided a list of possible contacts, including the Lim Clan Association at 12 Lorong 24A Geylang Road. I have written to the association but have not yet received a reply. I will follow up by phone next week.

**Genealogical Research Notebook (GRN-2024)**

**Entry date: 2024-07-15 (Monday)**

**Meeting with the Federation of Genealogical Research Institutes (FGRI) — Data Sharing Protocols**

Attendees: Marcus Lim (Project Lead), Evelyn Tan (Research Associate), Dr. Priya Nair (FGRI, Director of Digital Archives), Mr. Cheng Wei Ming (FGRI, Legal Counsel).

Location: FGRI office, 3rd floor, 12 Robinson Road, Singapore 068912. Meeting commenced at 10:00 hrs SGT and concluded at 11:45 hrs SGT.

Purpose: To discuss the draft data sharing agreement between the Lim Family History Project and FGRI, and to clarify the technical and procedural requirements for the exchange of genealogical records.

**Summary of discussion:**

1. **Scope of data to be shared.** Dr. Nair confirmed that FGRI is willing to share digitised copies of the following categories of records held in their collection, subject to the terms of the agreement:
   - Straits Settlements land records (1880–1940), specifically those relating to properties in the Geylang and Katong areas.
   - Chinese burial ground registers for the former Peck San Theng cemetery (now part of Bidadari estate).
   - A small set of family pedigree charts donated by the Lim Kongsi in 1987, which Dr. Nair believes may contain entries relevant to our Lim Ah Kow research line.

Marcus requested that FGRI also consider sharing the index cards for the 1921 and 1931 Singapore census (where extant). Mr. Cheng noted that the census index cards are not held by FGRI; they are under the purview of the National Archives of Singapore. He suggested we approach NAS separately. Noted.

2. **Format and delivery method.** FGRI prefers to provide data as PDF/A files for scanned documents, and as CSV files for structured data such as burial registers. Dr. Nair mentioned that the CSV files for the burial ground registers include the following fields: Surname, Given Name, Age at Death, Date of Burial (in the format DD/MM/YYYY), Plot Number, and Remarks. The Remarks field often contains notes such as "no headstone" or "family plot". We agreed that this format is acceptable.

For the pedigree charts, FGRI will provide high-resolution scans (600 dpi) in TIFF format. Marcus asked whether OCR text files could accompany the scans; Mr. Cheng said this would be possible for the typed portions of the charts, but handwritten annotations would not be OCR'd. We accepted this limitation.

3. **Restrictions on use.** Mr. Cheng explained that FGRI's data sharing policy requires that any material supplied under the agreement be used solely for non-commercial genealogical research. Publication of derived findings (including in a planned family history book) is permitted, provided that FGRI is acknowledged in the credits. The draft agreement contains a clause (Clause 7.2) stating that FGRI must receive a copy of any publication that cites their records at least two weeks prior to distribution. Marcus asked whether this applies to internal working papers; Mr. Cheng confirmed that it does not — only to external publications.

We also discussed the handling of personal data of living individuals. Mr. Cheng noted that the burial registers and land records are all more than 80 years old, so the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) is not expected to be a barrier. However, he advised that if any record contains the name of a person believed to be living, we should redact the name before sharing findings publicly. We agreed to adopt this practice.

4. **Technical access.** Dr. Nair offered to set up a secure FTP folder for the transfer of the first batch of files. She will send the login credentials and a folder structure guide by email within the next three working days. The folder structure will be as follows:
   - /Land_Records/
   - /Burial_Registers/
   - /Pedigree_Charts/
   - /Correspondence/

We will upload any requests or queries to the /Correspondence/ folder, and FGRI will respond within five working days.

5. **Timeline.** Dr. Nair estimated that the first batch of files (land records and burial registers) can be prepared by 12 August 2024. The pedigree charts will take longer, as they require careful handling; estimated delivery by 30 September 2024. Marcus asked whether the pedigree charts could be scanned sooner if we agreed to accept a lower resolution; Dr. Nair declined, citing preservation concerns. We accepted the timeline.

The application itself was straightforward, but the supporting materials took longer than expected. I included:

1. A cover letter addressed to the GSS Accreditation Committee
2. The completed application form (Form GSS-ACC-2024, revised January 2024)
3. My current CV (updated March 2024, with the new publication on the Lim lineage)
4. Two letters of recommendation — one from Dr. Ahmad Fauzi (National University of Singapore) and one from Ms. Rachel Tan (President, Singapore Heritage Society)
5. A list of my published research (12 items total, including the 2023 article in the Journal of Southeast Asian Genealogy)
6. The draft submission checklist — which I need to finalize

**Items still pending for the GSS review:**
- Final version of the submission checklist (due 22 March)
- Updated community engagement section (Evelyn said she could help with this)
- Any additional documentation the committee requests after their initial review

---

**Marriage Record — Lim Family (1892):**

I found the marriage record at the National Archives yesterday afternoon. It was in the Straits Settlements records, which makes sense given the time period. The record is dated 12 June 1892, and it lists:

- Groom: Lim Ah Kow (age 26, merchant)
- Bride: Tan Swee Neo (age 19, no occupation listed)
- Witnesses: Lim Cheng Hoe and Tan Kim Seng
- Location: St. Andrew's Cathedral, Singapore

This is significant because it connects the Lim and Tan families directly. I've been trying to establish this connection for months.

**Next steps for this line:**
- Cross-reference with the church records at St. Andrew's (the National Archives copy is a transcription, so I need to check the original)
- Look for the couple's marriage certificate in the Registrar-General's records
- Search for birth records of their children (likely 1893–1910)

---

**Tan Family Branch — Progress Update:**

Evelyn sent me an email this morning with a lead on the Tan family. She found a reference to "Tan Swee Neo" in a 1905 directory of Singapore merchants. The directory lists her as the widow of Lim Ah Kow, which confirms that Lim Ah Kow died sometime between 1892 and 1905.

On 15 March, Marcus Lim submitted_application_to Genealogical Society of Singapore. Record status: current.

**Key details from the directory:**
- Name: Tan Swee Neo (widow of Lim Ah Kow)
- Address: 14 Telok Ayer Street
- Occupation: Merchant (continuing her husband's business)
- Notes: Listed as "proprietor of Lim Ah Kow & Co."

This is useful, but I need to find the exact date of Lim Ah Kow's death. I'll check the burial records at Bukit Brown Cemetery and the Straits Settlements death records.

**Possible leads:**
- Bukit Brown Cemetery records (available at the National Archives)
- Straits Settlements death records (1880–1910)
- Probate records for Lim Ah Kow (likely in the Supreme Court records)

---

**DNA Test Results — Interpretation:**

I received the DNA test results from the lab earlier this week. The results are for the sample I submitted in February (sample ID: LFHP-DNA-2024-02).

**Summary of results:**
- Y-DNA haplogroup: O-M122 (common in southern China)
- mtDNA haplogroup: M7 (also common in southern China)
- Autosomal DNA: 92% East Asian, 5% Southeast Asian, 3% unassigned

**Interpretation notes:**
- The Y-DNA haplogroup is consistent with the Lim family's documented origins in Fujian Province, China
- The mtDNA haplogroup suggests the maternal line also originated in southern China
- The 5% Southeast Asian component could indicate some degree of local admixture — this is worth investigating further

**Caveats:**
- These results are statistical estimates, not definitive proof of ancestry
- The unassigned 3% may resolve with future updates to the reference database
- I should compare these results with the samples from other family members (Evelyn's father and my cousin) when they arrive

I followed up with Dr. Natalie Wong at the California lab in early September, as I had planned. The reference database update she expected in June was delayed, but it finally went live on 2 September. She re-ran the Y-DNA haplogroup analysis for Marcus's sample. The result remains O-M122, which is consistent with the Fujian origin. She also noted that the subclade prediction has improved slightly — the new database suggests a more specific branch (O-M122\* with a possible link to the Minnan cluster), but she cautioned that the resolution is still not sufficient for a confident subclade assignment. She recommended we consider a deeper SNP test in the new year if we want to narrow the geographic origin further. I have added this to the list of pending tasks for Q1 2025.

Evelyn's autosomal results have also been updated. The unassigned 3% that we had been tracking has now been resolved: 2% is assigned to the "Southern China" reference population, and 1% remains unassigned. Dr. Wong explained that this residual unassigned portion is common for individuals with significant admixture from historically underrepresented populations. No further action is needed on this.

**Newspaper Search — Death Date of Lim Ah Kow**

The search for Lim Ah Kow's death date has been a slow but steady process. Since my last entry, I have continued working through the digitised newspapers on NewspaperSG, focusing on the *Straits Times* and *Malaya Tribune* for the period 1932–1935. The two leads I noted in June have both been resolved:

- The 14 March 1930 death notice for a "Lim Ah Kow" of Kampong Java Road, aged 61, is not our man. The age does not match, and the address, while in the same area, is not one we have linked to the family. I have marked this lead as closed.
- The 22 November 1931 death notice for a "Lim Ah Kow" of River Valley Road remains a strong lead. The clearer scan I requested from the National Library (reference NL/REF/2024/0831) arrived on 12 September. The notice reads: "Lim Ah Kow, of 14 River Valley Road, passed away peacefully at his residence on 21 November 1931, aged 44. Funeral to leave on 23 November at 3 p.m." The age of 44 would be consistent with a birth year of 1887, which does not match our Lim Ah Kow (born 1911). However, I have not ruled it out entirely, because the death notice may have been placed by a relative with the same name. I have requested the death certificate from the Registry of Births and Deaths; the reference is RBD/2024/1042. I expect a response within two weeks.

I have also searched for obituaries in the *Singapore Free Press* and the *Pinang Gazette* for the period 1928–1935, but the OCR quality is poor and the search has not yielded any new leads. I will pause the newspaper search until the death certificate request comes back.

**Genealogical Research Notebook (GRN-2024)**

**Entry date: 2024-07-15 (Monday)**

**Meeting with the Federation of Genealogical Research Institutes (FGRI) — Data Sharing Protocols**

Attendees: Marcus Lim (Project Lead), Evelyn Tan (Research Associate), Dr. Priya Nair (FGRI, Director of Digital Archives), Mr. Cheng Wei Ming (FGRI, Legal Counsel).

Location: FGRI office, 3rd floor, 12 Robinson Road, Singapore 068912. Meeting commenced at 10:00 hrs SGT and concluded at 11:45 hrs SGT.

Purpose: To discuss the draft data sharing agreement between the Lim Family History Project and FGRI, and to clarify the technical and procedural requirements for the exchange of genealogical records.

**Summary of discussion:**

1. **Scope of data to be shared.** Dr. Nair confirmed that FGRI is willing to share digitised copies of the following categories of records held in their collection, subject to the terms of the agreement:
   - Straits Settlements land records (1880–1940), specifically those relating to properties in the Geylang and Katong areas.
   - Chinese burial ground registers for the former Peck San Theng cemetery (now part of Bidadari estate).
   - A small set of family pedigree charts donated by the Lim Kongsi in 1987, which Dr. Nair believes may contain entries relevant to our Lim Ah Kow research line.

Marcus requested that FGRI also consider sharing the index cards for the 1921 and 1931 Singapore census (where extant). Mr. Cheng noted that the census index cards are not held by FGRI; they are under the purview of the National Archives of Singapore. He suggested we approach NAS separately. Noted.

2. **Format and delivery method.** FGRI prefers to provide data as PDF/A files for scanned documents, and as CSV files for structured data such as burial registers. Dr. Nair mentioned that the CSV files for the burial ground registers include the following fields: Surname, Given Name, Age at Death, Date of Burial (in the format DD/MM/YYYY), Plot Number, and Remarks. The Remarks field often contains notes such as "no headstone" or "family plot". We agreed that this format is acceptable.

For the pedigree charts, FGRI will provide high-resolution scans (600 dpi) in TIFF format. Marcus asked whether OCR text files could accompany the scans; Mr. Cheng said this would be possible for the typed portions of the charts, but handwritten annotations would not be OCR'd. We accepted this limitation.

3. **Restrictions on use.** Mr. Cheng explained that FGRI's data sharing policy requires that any material supplied under the agreement be used solely for non-commercial genealogical research. Publication of derived findings (including in a planned family history book) is permitted, provided that FGRI is acknowledged in the credits. The draft agreement contains a clause (Clause 7.2) stating that FGRI must receive a copy of any publication that cites their records at least two weeks prior to distribution. Marcus asked whether this applies to internal working papers; Mr. Cheng confirmed that it does not — only to external publications.

We also discussed the handling of personal data of living individuals. Mr. Cheng noted that the burial registers and land records are all more than 80 years old, so the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) is not expected to be a barrier. However, he advised that if any record contains the name of a person believed to be living, we should redact the name before sharing findings publicly. We agreed to adopt this practice.

4. **Technical access.** Dr. Nair offered to set up a secure FTP folder for the transfer of the first batch of files. She will send the login credentials and a folder structure guide by email within the next three working days. The folder structure will be as follows:
   - /Land_Records/
   - /Burial_Registers/
   - /Pedigree_Charts/
   - /Correspondence/

We will upload any requests or queries to the /Correspondence/ folder, and FGRI will respond within five working days.

5. **Timeline.** Dr. Nair estimated that the first batch of files (land records and burial registers) can be prepared by 12 August 2024. The pedigree charts will take longer, as they require careful handling; estimated delivery by 30 September 2024. Marcus asked whether the pedigree charts could be scanned sooner if we agreed to accept a lower resolution; Dr. Nair declined, citing preservation concerns. We accepted the timeline.
